title: 6: p-values and t-tests
text:
Recall

CI calculations assume we know the true mean (\(\mu\))
If actually we knew what \(\mu\) is, then we can calculate probability of experiment
However, we don’t actually know \(\mu\), so we can’t actually calculate probability.
This is why we can’t use probability words in our CI interpretations

title: 6: p-values and t-tests
text:
Solution: pretend we know \(\mu\)

Don’t make any assumptions about \(\mu\)

❌ Cannot calculate probabilities
\(\rightarrow\) CIs

Pretend that we know \(\mu\)

✅ Can calculate probabilities
\(\rightarrow\) p-values

title: 6: p-values and t-tests
text:
We will pretend to know \(\mu\). What does this mean?
This means that we can simulate what the sampling distribution would look like if we assume our pretend \(\mu\) is true.
What are good \(\mu\)’s to assume?

title: 6: p-values and t-tests
text:
What \(\mu\) to assume?
If we are interested in proving A, we cannot assume A.


A circular argument: You cannot prove something if you already assume it is true.
Examples of circular arguments:

I trust you because you are trustworthy
The scientific method works because science tells me so
Calibrating a compass by only using that one compass.

You need to use a second compass or known landmarks (like the stars).

title: 6: p-values and t-tests
text:
Null hypothesis testing

You need to make sure the pretend \(\mu\) is different from the one you are actually interested in “proving”.
This is the purpose of a null hypothesis

The “opposite” hypothesis of your main hypothesis

If our results are very different from the null hypothesis, then we falsify it.

title: 6: p-values and t-tests
text:
Let’s say in our experiment, we want to show that there is a difference between two groups.
Alternative hypothesis: there is a difference between groups.
The opposite of the alternative hypothesis would be that there is no difference between the groups. AKA the difference = 0.
The opposite of the alternative hypothesis is the null hypothesis.

title: 6: p-values and t-tests
text:
Definition of p-value


The p-value is the probability of observing our results (or something more extreme) given that our null hypothesis is true.

title: 6: p-values and t-tests
text:
p-value summary

Assumes null hypothesis is true
Create a sampling distribution from the null hypothesis
Compare actual observed difference to the opposite sampling distribution (null sampling distribution)
The area under the curve outside of the observed differences line is the p-value

title: 7: Paired data and t-tests
text:
Summary

When you calculate the overall difference between the samples, that leads to a wider sampling distribution.
When you calculate individual differences first, it leads to a narrower sampling distribution.
This matches our intuition that when we only calculate overall difference, it leads to less certainty, and when we calculate the individual differences, it leads to more certainty.




Overall differences \(\rightarrow\) less certainty












Individual differences \(\rightarrow\) more certainty

title: Descriptive vs. inferential statistics
text:
Interpreting descriptive statistics

Shape (skew)

All three samples are somewhat bell shaped. There is no clear skew in any of the plots.

Spread

All three samples have similar similar widths,. None are clearly wider than the other.

Center (optional)

In all three samples, the score is centered at around 10.
Note: Performance score, not just performance.

title: Descriptive vs. inferential statistics
text:
❓ Which interpretation is the best?

HistogramsAnswer optionsExplanations














Both plots are bell shaped, with the second plot being slightly more skewed. The first plot is slightly narrower than the second. The score is centered at around 5 for the first plot, whereas it is centered at around 7 for the second plot. (correct)
The second plot is significantly more skewed than the first plot. It is also significantly wider. Both plots are bell shaped. Memory levels for the second group is higher, with a mean of 7, than for the first group, with a mean of 5.
Both plots are rather bell shaped, though the second plot may be more skewed and is slightly wider than the first plot. The memory levels for the second group is higher than for the first group, at about 7, whereas the first group has a lower memory level, at about 5.
Both plots are bell shaped. The second plot is slightly wider and slightly more skewed than the first plot. (correct)




1 includes talking about the shape, spread, and center, without making claims about the popultion.
2 is wrong because it uses the word “significant”, which implies a population level conclusion.
3 is wrong because it makes a strong statement about a group difference. Without specifying that the difference is in the the score, not just memory levels, it doesn’t specify that it is only in these samples.
4 avoids any issues with interpreting the “center” by not talking about it at all. Remember that in this class, describing the “center” is optional for descriptive plots.

title: Descriptive vs. inferential statistics
text:
Guessing game: I have take a random sample from either Population A or Population B. Which population does this random sample come from?

“Population” = The true distribution

title: Descriptive vs. inferential statistics
text: I took a second random sample from either Population A or Population B. Which distribution does this random sample come from?

title: Descriptive vs. inferential statistics
text:
Statistical tests must be used

It can be hard to tell which population the sample came from!
Instead of asking, “do we know for sure which distribution the sample comes from?”, can we instead ask “what is the probability that the sample comes from A or B?”

Kind of. There isn’t a way to exactly calculate the probability, but we can still capture this intution with the idea of “confidence”.

We must use some sort of test, like confidence intervals or t-tests, to infer something about the true population (more on CIs next week)

title: 4: Sampling distributions and CIs
text:
Confidence intervals



 




Using the sampling distribution, we know that:

If the true mean is \(\mu\), then there is a 95% chance that \(\bar{x}\) is between \(\mu - 1.96 \times SE\) and \(\mu + 1.96 \times SE\).

But we can’t calculate \(\mu \pm 1.96 \times SE\) because we don’t know \(\mu\).

title: 4: Sampling distributions and CIs
text:

Assuming that the true mean is \(\mu\)
\(P(\mu - 1.96SE < \bar{x} < \mu + 1.96SE) = P(\bar{x} - 1.96SE < \mu < \bar{x} + 1.96SE)\)
